source_text: Βραχὺς καὶ τοῖς ὤμοις ἐνδεδυκὼς ὁ τράχηλος τῆς ἄρκτου· καὶ λέοντος δὲ, καὶ τίγριδος, καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν, ὅσα τούτου τοῦ γένους· ὅτι οὐκ ἐκ τῆς πόας αὐτοῖς ἡ τροφὴ, οὐδὲ ἀνάγκη πρὸς τὴν γῆν κατακύπτειν, σαρκοφάγοις οὖσι, καὶ ἐκ τῆς ἄγρας τῶν ζῴων διαρκουμένοις. Τί βούλεται ἡ προνομαία τῷ ἐλέφαντι; Ὅτι μέγα τὸ ζῷον, καὶ τῶν χερσαίων τὸ μέγιστον, εἰς τὴν τῶν ἐντυγχανόντων ἔκπληξιν παραχθὲν, πολύσαρκον ἐχρῆν εἶναι καὶ συμπεφορημένον τὸ σῶμα. Τούτῳ εἰ μέγας καὶ ἀναλογῶν τοῖς ποσὶν ὁ τράχηλος προσετέθη, δυσμεταχείριστος ἂν ἦν, τῷ ὑπερβάλλοντι βάρει καταρρέπων ἀεὶ πρὸς τὸ κάτω. Νῦν δὲ ἡ μὲν κεφαλὴ δι' ὀλίγων τῶν τοῦ αὐχένος σφονδύλων πρὸς τὴν ῥάχιν συνάπτεται· ἔχει δὲ τὴν προνομαίαν, τὴν τοῦ τραχήλου χρείαν ἀποπληροῦσαν, δι' ἧς καὶ τὴν τροφὴν προσάγεται, καὶ τὸ ποτὸν ἀνιμᾶται. Ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀδιάρθρωτοι αὐτῷ οἱ πόδες, οἱονεὶ κίονες ἡνωμένοι, τὸ βάρος ὑποστηρίζουσιν. Εἰ γὰρ χαῦνα αὐτῷ καὶ δίυγρα ὑπετέθη τὰ κῶλα, συνεχεῖς ἂν ἐγίνοντο τῶν ἄρθρων αἱ ἐκτροπαὶ, συνοκλάζοντος καὶ διανισταμένου κουφίζειν τὸ βάρος μὴ ἐξαρκούντων. Νῦν δὲ βραχὺς ἀστράγαλος ὑπόκειται τῷ ποδὶ τοῦ ἐλέφαντος, οὔτε μέντοι εἰς ἀγκύλην, οὔτε εἰς γόνυ διήρθρωται. Οὐ γὰρ ἂν ὑπήνεγκε τὸ τῶν ἄρθρων ὀλισθηρὸν τὴν πολυσαρκίαν τοῦ ζῴου πολλὴν αὐτῷ περικεχυμένην καὶ περιτρέμουσαν. Ὅθεν χρεία γέγονε τοῦ μυκτῆρος ἐκείνου μέχρι ποδῶν καθιεμένου. Οὐχ ὁρᾷς ἐν τοῖς πολέμοις, ὅτι οἱονεὶ πύργοι τινὲς ἔμψυχοι τῆς φάλαγγος προηγοῦνται; ἢ βουνοί τινες σάρκινοι, ἀνυπόστατον ἔχοντες τὴν ὁρμὴν, τῶν ἐναντίων τὸν συνασπισμὸν διακόπτουτιν; Οἷς εἰ μὴ ἦν ἀναλογοῦντα τὰ κάτω, πρὸς οὐδένα ἂν χρόνον τὸ ζῷον διήρκεσε. Νῦν δὲ ἤδη τινὲς ἱστοροῦσι καὶ τριακόσια ἔτη καὶ πλείω τούτων βιοῦν τὸν ἐλέφαντα· διὰ τοῦτο συμπεπηγὸς καὶ οὐ διηρθρωμένον τὰ κῶλα. Τὴν δὲ τροφὴν, ὥσπερ ἔφαμεν, ἡ προνομαία χαμόθεν ἐπὶ τὸ ὕψος διακομίζει, ὀφιώδης τις οὖσα καὶ ὑγροτέρα τὴν φύσιν. Οὕτως ἀληθὴς ὁ λόγος, ὅτι οὐδὲν περιττὸν οὐδὲ ἐλλεῖπον ἐν τοῖς κτισθεῖσι δυνατὸν εὑρεθῆναι. Τοῦτο μέντοι τοσοῦτον ὂν τῷ μεγέθει ὑποχείριον ἡμῖν κατέστησεν ὁ Θεὸς (ὥστε καὶ διδασκόμενον συνιέναι, καὶ τυπτόμενον καταδέχεσθαι), ἐναργῶς ἡμᾶς ἐκδιδάσκων, ὅτι πάντα ὑπέταξεν ἡμῖν, διὰ τὸ κατ' εἰκόνα ἡμᾶς πεποιῆσθαι τοῦ κτίσαντος. Οὐ μόνον δὲ ἐν τοῖς μεγάλοις τῶν ζῴων τὴν ἀνεξιχνίαστον σοφίαν ἔξεστι κατιδεῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τοῖς μικροτάτοις οὐδὲν ἔλαττον συναγεῖραι τὸ θαῦμα. Ὥσπερ γὰρ οὐ μᾶλλον θαυμάζω τὰς μεγάλας τῶν ὀρῶν κορυφὰς, αἳ τῷ πλησίον εἶναι τῶν νεφῶν τῇ συνεχεῖ περιπνοίᾳ διασώζουσι τὸ χειμέριον, ἢ τὴν ἐν ταῖς φάραγξι κοιλότητα, οὐ μόνον τὸ δυσήνεμον τῶν ὑψηλῶν διαφεύγουσαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀλεεινὸν ἀεὶ τὸν ἀέρα συνέχουσαν· οὕτως καὶ ἐν ταῖς τῶν ζῴων κατασκευαῖς οὐ μᾶλλον ἄγαμαι τὸν ἐλέφαντα τοῦ μεγέθους, ἢ τὸν μῦν, ὅτι φοβερός ἐστι τῷ ἐλέφαντι· ἢ τὸ λεπτότατον τοῦ σκορπίου κέντρον, πῶς ἐκοίλανεν ὥσπερ αὐλὸν ὁ τεχνίτης, ὥστε δι' αὐτοῦ τὸν ἰὸν τοῖς τρωθεῖσιν ἐνίεσθαι. Καὶ μηδεὶς ἐγκαλείτω τούτου ἕνεκεν τῷ ποιητῇ, ὅτι ἰοβόλα ζῷα καὶ φθαρτικὰ καὶ πολέμια τῇ ζωῇ ἡμῶν ἐπεισήγαγεν· ἢ οὕτω δ' ἄν τις καὶ παιδαγωγῷ ἐγκαλοίη εἰς τάξιν ἄγοντι τὴν εὐκολίαν τῆς νεότητος, καὶ πληγαῖς καὶ μάστιξι τὸ ἀκόλαστον σωφρονίζοντι.
thought_title: The elephant's fitted frame and the wisdom in small creatures
orientation: Basil is still describing how God fitted each land animal's body to its food and life, and now turns to the bear, lion, tiger, and especially the elephant, before drawing a lesson about God's wisdom in both great and small creatures.
pass_a_gloss: Short and sunk into the shoulders is the neck of the bear; and of the lion, and of the tiger, and of the rest, as many as are of this kind; because their food is not from grass, nor is there necessity to bend down to the earth, since they are flesh-eaters and are sustained from the hunt of animals. What does the trunk mean for the elephant? Because the animal is great, and the greatest of the land animals, brought forth for the terror of those who encounter it, the body had to be fleshy and compacted. If to this animal a great neck, proportionate to the feet, had been added, it would have been hard to manage, always tipping down by its excessive weight toward the lower part. But as it is, the head is joined to the spine through few vertebrae of the neck; and it has the trunk, fulfilling the need of the neck, through which it both brings food to itself and draws up drink. But also its feet are unjointed, like united pillars, supporting the weight. For if loose and watery limbs had been placed under it, the dislocations of the joints would have been continuous, since they would not be sufficient to lighten the weight when it crouches down and rises up. But as it is, a short ankle-bone lies under the foot of the elephant, yet it is not jointed either into a bend or into a knee. For the slipperiness of the joints would not have borne the great fleshiness of the animal poured around it and trembling around it. For this reason there came to be need of that trunk let down as far as the feet. Do you not see in wars, that like certain living towers they lead the phalanx? Or certain fleshy hills, having an irresistible onset, they cut through the shield-wall of the enemy? If the lower parts were not proportionate to these, the animal would not have lasted for any time. But as it is, already some report that the elephant lives even three hundred years and more than these; for this reason its limbs are compacted and not jointed. And its food, as we said, the trunk carries up from the ground to the height, being serpent-like and rather moist in nature. So true is the saying, that nothing superfluous nor lacking in the things created can be found. This animal, though so great in size, God made subject to us (so that both when taught it understands, and when struck it submits), clearly teaching us that he subjected all things to us, because we have been made according to the image of the Creator. And not only in the great animals is it possible to behold the unsearchable wisdom, but also in the smallest ones it is possible to gather no less the wonder. For just as I do not more admire the great peaks of the mountains, which by being near the clouds preserve the wintry condition by the continual blowing around them, than the hollow in the ravines, which not only escapes the windiness of the heights but also always holds the air warm; so also in the constructions of the animals I do not more admire the elephant for its size than the mouse, because it is fearsome to the elephant; or the very fine sting of the scorpion, how the craftsman hollowed it like a pipe, so that through it the poison is injected into those who are wounded. And let no one accuse the Maker on account of this, that he introduced venomous and destructive animals and enemies to our life; or in this way one might also accuse a tutor who brings the ease of youth into order, and by blows and whips disciplines the unruly.

choices.why: The standard anatomical term for the elephant's proboscis; 'trunk' is the natural English equivalent and avoids the archaic 'proboscis'.
The verb συμφορέω means to heap or mass together; 'compacted' captures the dense, solid body Basil contrasts with loose limbs.
ἀνυπόστατος means 'not to be withstood'; 'irresistible onset' preserves the military force of ὁρμή.
The term refers to the close-locked shields of a phalanx; 'shield-wall' conveys the military image in plain English.
The glossary fixes εἰκὼν as 'image'; the phrase echoes Genesis 1:26 and must keep the fixed rendering.
The παιδαγωγός in antiquity was a slave who supervised and disciplined a child; 'tutor' is the closest plain English term without the modern schoolteacher connotation.

pass_b_english: The bear's neck is short and sunk into its shoulders, and so is the lion's, and the tiger's, and the rest of that kind, because their food does not come from grass and they have no need to bend down to the ground, since they are flesh-eaters and sustain themselves by hunting other animals. What is the purpose of the elephant's trunk? Because the animal is large—the largest of the land animals—and was brought forth to terrify whatever it meets, its body had to be massive and compacted. If a neck as large and proportionate to its feet had been added to this body, the animal would have been hard to manage, always dragged downward by its excessive weight. As it is, the head is joined to the spine by only a few vertebrae of the neck, and it has the trunk, which fulfills the function of a neck: through it the elephant brings food to its mouth and draws up its drink. Its feet, moreover, are unjointed, like solid pillars, to support the weight. For if its limbs had been set beneath it loose and flexible, its joints would have been constantly dislocated, since they could not bear the weight when the animal crouched down and rose up again. As it is, a short ankle-bone lies under the elephant's foot, and it is not jointed either at the bend or at the knee. For the slipperiness of joints could never have endured the great mass of flesh poured around the animal and quivering on every side. Hence the need for that trunk that reaches down to its feet. Do you not see in wars how they go before the battle-line like living towers, or like hills of flesh, and with their irresistible onset they break through the shield-wall of the enemy? If their lower parts were not proportionate, the animal would not have survived for any length of time. As it is, some report that the elephant lives three hundred years and more; for this reason its limbs are solidly fixed and not jointed. Its food, as we said, the trunk carries up from the ground to the height—a trunk that is serpent-like and rather supple by nature. So true is the saying that nothing superfluous and nothing lacking can be found among created things. This animal, though so great in size, God has made subject to us—so much so that it understands when taught and submits when struck—clearly teaching us that he has subjected all things to us, because we have been made according to the image of the Creator (Genesis 1:26). And not only in the large animals is it possible to behold the unsearchable wisdom of God; in the very smallest, no less, we can gather the same wonder. For just as I do not marvel more at the great peaks of the mountains, which by being near the clouds preserve their wintry character through constant exposure to the winds, than at the hollow in the ravines, which not only escapes the harsh winds of the heights but also keeps the air always warm—so also in the construction of animals I do not admire the elephant for its size more than the mouse, because the mouse is feared by the elephant; or the scorpion's very fine sting, how the Craftsman hollowed it out like a pipe, so that through it the venom is injected into those who are struck. And let no one accuse the Maker on this account, that he has introduced venomous and destructive creatures that are hostile to our life. Otherwise one might as well accuse a tutor who brings the easy-going ways of youth into order and disciplines what is undisciplined with blows and whips.

problems.why: ἀγκύλη means 'bend/curve' or specifically 'elbow' in animals; 'hock' is a specific joint in horses (tarsal), but elephants don't have hocks. The Greek refers to the elbow-like bend in the leg, not a hock. Better 'bend' or 'elbow'.

edits.old: either at the hock or at the knee
edits.new: either at the bend or at the knee

fixed: Changed 'hock' to 'bend' because ἀγκύλη means 'bend/curve' or 'elbow' in animals, not the equine hock; elephants do not have hocks.

last_rejected.quote: and it is not jointed either at the bend or at the knee
last_rejected.source_quote: οὔτε μὲντοι εἰς ἀγκύλην, οὔτε εἰς γόνυ διήρθρωται
last_rejected.why: Source has 'οὔτε μέντοι' = 'and yet not' — adversative 'yet' is dropped, softening the point.
last_rejected.fix: and yet it is not jointed either at the bend or at the knee
last_rejected.ruling: μέντοι is a particle with range from 'indeed' to 'yet'; 'and...not' captures normal adversative force adequately.

last_rejected.quote: its body had to be massive and compacted
last_rejected.source_quote: πολύσαρκον ἐχρῆν εἶναι καὶ συμπεφορημένον τὸ σῶμα
last_rejected.why: "compacted" suggests compressed/dense; συμπεφορημένον means heaped up/piled together, i.e., bulky, massive in bulk
last_rejected.fix: its body had to be fleshy and bulky
last_rejected.ruling: συμπεφορημένον = brought/bound together; 'compacted' is within normal range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.why: ἡνωμένοι means "united/joined together" not "solid"; the point is continuous unjointed columns, not solidity
last_rejected.fix: like columns joined in one piece
last_rejected.ruling: ἡνωμένοι = united/joined; 'solid' as 'continuous/unjointed' is acceptable, not a real error.

last_rejected.why: "loose and flexible" is too neutral; χαῦνα means porous/spongy/loose-textured, δίυγρα means moist/watery—both suggest weak, yielding structure unable to bear weight
last_rejected.ruling: χαῦνα = loose, δίυγρα = moist; 'loose and flexible' captures the sense adequately for the argument.

last_rejected.why: ὀλισθηρὸν means "liable to slip/dislocate" not "slipperiness"; it's instability, not a surface quality
last_rejected.fix: the tendency of joints to slip
last_rejected.ruling: ὀλισθηρὸν = slippery/labile; 'slipperiness' conveys the instability idea without misleading the reader.

last_rejected.why: "poured around" suggests liquid; περικεχυμένην means spread around/poured over, but here describes flesh distributed over the body
last_rejected.ruling: περικεχυμένην from χέω = poured around/spread; 'poured around' is literal and not misleading in context.

last_rejected.why: περιτρέμουσαν means trembling/shaking all over, not "on every side" (which suggests direction, not motion)
last_rejected.ruling: περιτρέμουσαν = trembling all over; 'quivering on every side' conveys the same meaning adequately.

last_rejected.quote: that trunk that reaches down to its feet
last_rejected.source_quote: τοῦ μυκτῆρος ἐκείνου μέχρι ποδῶν καθιεμένου
last_rejected.why: μυκτήρ means "nose/snout" not "trunk" (προνομαία is trunk); this refers to the trunk reaching to the feet, but "that trunk" is unclear—it's "that nose/snout" reaching down
last_rejected.fix: that nose reaching down to its feet
last_rejected.ruling: μυκτήρ = nose/snout; 'trunk' is the standard English term for an elephant's snout, not a real error.

last_rejected.why: Missing subject: "they" refers to elephants, but Greek has no explicit subject—English needs "the elephants" or "these creatures"
last_rejected.fix: the elephants go before the battle-line
last_rejected.ruling: Greek προηγοῦνται has implied subject from context; 'they' correctly refers to elephants without ambiguity.

last_rejected.why: σάρκινοι means "fleshy/made of flesh" not "of flesh" as material; "fleshy hills" or "hills of living flesh"
last_rejected.ruling: σάρκινοι = made of flesh; 'hills of flesh' is a natural English rendering, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.why: ἀνυπόστατον means "irresistible/unstoppable" but the phrase is "having irresistible onset/impetus"—English splits this awkwardly
last_rejected.ruling: ἀνυπόστατον ἔχοντες τὴν ὁρμήν = having irresistible onset; English conveys this accurately despite slight awkwardness.

last_rejected.why: κοιλότητα is singular "hollow/valley" not generic "hollow"; "the hollow in the ravines" is unclear—better "the hollows in the ravines" or "the valley-bottom"
last_rejected.ruling: κοιλότητα singular = hollow; 'the hollow in the ravines' is grammatically acceptable and not misleading.
